summaries.headline: Labor Department Bets $162M on Apprenticeship Outcomes
summaries.summary: The U.S. Department of Labor has awarded nearly $162 million through five cooperative agreements to expand Registered Apprenticeship programs in AI infrastructure, semiconductors, nuclear energy, IT, telecommunications, shipbuilding and automotive technician roles. The funding flows through a Pay-for-Performance model that pays sponsors as apprentices hit verified retention and progression milestones rather than for upfront enrollment, with recipients including FloridaCommerce, Jobs for the Future, the Wireless Infrastructure Association, Clark University and the ASE Education Foundation. For K-12 leaders building career pathway partnerships, the outcomes-based structure signals where federal workforce dollars are headed and which industry sectors are positioning themselves to recruit directly from high school and postsecondary pipelines.

summaries.headline: The Lexington Problem: Beating the Literacy Odds Without the Science of Reading
Absenteeism Fixes Arrive Too Late, Advocates Argue
summaries.summary: Chronic absenteeism affects roughly 22-24 percent of students nationally, well above the pre-pandemic rate of about 15 percent, and district responses like home visits and automated messaging tend to target students only after disengagement has already taken hold. Research links persistent absences to anxiety, depression, trauma, and weakened school connection, with a 2023 survey citing mental health as a leading cause of missed school days and Johns Hopkins researchers naming health challenges among the most common drivers. The push now is for districts to adopt evidence-based SEL screening tools that flag disengagement patterns early, before attendance data alone can capture the problem.

summaries.headline: Denver Board, Superintendent Clash Over Governance Lines
summaries.summary: Denver Public Schools Superintendent Alex Marrero sent a June email alleging that the school board is overstepping into administrative matters, leaving him caught between disputes among members and warning that "the current trajectory" has become "increasingly untenable." Board President Xóchitl Gaytán has scheduled a July 27 special meeting after several members requested a discussion of his concerns, and confirmed Marrero's email was not intended to trigger a contract clause that would let him treat major governance changes as effective termination — a move that would otherwise entitle him to 12 months of his $346,529 salary. The dispute centers on policy governance language requiring the board to set goals without directing how staff carries them out, a tension playing out as Marrero has reportedly applied for a superintendent opening in Florida.

summaries.headline: NYC Halts Software Buys Amid AI Backlash
summaries.summary: NYC Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels has asked principals to pause purchases of educational software until the Education Department finalizes its AI guidance later this summer, marking the most concrete restriction city officials have placed on ed-tech procurement to date. The move follows months of pushback after the department's initial March guidance drew criticism for doing too little to limit AI use, prompting more than half the City Council to back a moratorium and Samuels himself to admit the city "missed the mark"; the revised guidance, originally promised for June, has no new release date. The freeze signals that even as districts nationally rush to adopt AI tools, unresolved questions about student safety and data privacy can bring procurement to a standstill.

summaries.headline: Unpacking Absence Types Could Curb Chronic Absenteeism
summaries.summary: A new American Enterprise Institute report finds that most districts track chronic absenteeism in the aggregate, missing critical distinctions between excused and unexcused absences that could sharpen intervention strategies. Drawing on Indiana attendance data spanning the 2015-16 through 2023-24 school years, researchers identified distinct patterns tied to each absence type, suggesting the two categories often signal different underlying problems and require different responses. For district leaders still searching for traction against post-pandemic absenteeism rates, the data they already collect may hold more diagnostic power than they've been using.

summaries.headline: ISTE Defines What "AI-Ready" Actually Means
summaries.summary: ISTE+ASCD used its ISTELive 2026 conference to unveil an expanded Profile of an AI-Ready Graduate, moving beyond basic AI literacy frameworks to define the entry-level workforce skills students need on day one of a job. The profile identifies six roles students must embody to work alongside AI effectively — Learner, Researcher, Synthesizer, Problem Solver, Connector and Storyteller — each paired with concrete skills and practices, and it's built on the organization's existing Transformational Learning Principles and ISTE Standards for Students. For district leaders still treating AI instruction as tool training or policy compliance, the framework signals a shift toward embedding AI-specific competencies across every discipline as a graduation expectation, not an elective add-on.

summaries.headline: Six Months In, Mamdani's K-12 Agenda Stays Thin
summaries.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani has built his affordability agenda around childcare, transportation, and housing, leaving K-12 schools — the largest operation under his control by budget and headcount — largely on the sidelines. Of the hundreds of press releases his office has issued since January, only 11 touched K-12 education, and just one announced a genuinely new policy: an expansion of a curriculum overhaul that Chancellor Kamar Samuels inherited from the Adams administration. Longtime education advocates, including some Mamdani supporters, say the silence is notable given the scale of the system he oversees, and the coming months will test whether working groups and curriculum tweaks amount to a real strategy or just management of the status quo.

summaries.headline: Chicago Schools Find Workarounds to Save AP Jobs
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools moved to cut assistant principal funding this spring at more than 130 small schools with fewer than 250 students, part of an effort to close a $732.5 million deficit in its more than $10 billion budget. Most campuses avoided the cut: 72 schools tapped discretionary dollars to retain the position and another 23 won district exceptions, leaving roughly 40 schools without an assistant principal. The scramble underscores how central APs have become to daily operations in even the smallest buildings, and how quickly a formula-driven cut can collide with the on-the-ground realities principals and school leader unions are pushing districts to recognize in contract talks.

summaries.headline: NYC Tests Phone-Based Transit Cards for Students
summaries.summary: New York City's Education Department is piloting virtual student OMNY cards at seven schools, letting students tap their cellphones for transit rides instead of relying on physical cards, though officials haven't set a start date or disclosed which schools are involved. The move follows more than a year of talks with the MTA and responds to widespread complaints about paper OMNY cards that break easily and can take months to replace, leaving some students unable to afford fares and resorting to jumping turnstiles. Students without phones will still have access to physical cards, but the pilot signals a broader shift toward treating reliable transit access as an equity issue tied directly to school attendance.

summaries.headline: Outcomes-based contracting is a big shift for the edtech world
5 Questions About Security Debt for Higher Ed Institutions
Texas Educators Link STAAR Slide to Reading Habits
summaries.summary: Texas STAAR results show persistent reading struggles among students in grades three through six, and educators point to a web of causes beyond any single curriculum fix. A retired 30-year educator now tutoring in Temple says students increasingly report they don't read for fun, a gap she ties directly to weakening vocabulary and comprehension that then undermines performance across other tested subjects; one teacher told KWTX their district cut reading interventionists entirely, while others cite curriculum pacing that outstrips struggling readers. The pattern suggests literacy gaps are compounding through the accountability system rather than closing, raising the question of whether state and district programs are flexible enough to match how individual students actually learn to read.

summaries.headline: Pennsylvania's Overdue Budget Puts School Funding in Limbo
summaries.summary: Pennsylvania lawmakers returned to the Capitol this weekend to hash out a state budget now more than a week past its June 30 deadline, with public school funding for historically underfunded districts emerging as a central sticking point for House Democrats. Republicans are pushing back with priorities of their own, including expanded school choice funding and protection of the state's rainy day fund, while unrelated fights over skill game machines and data center regulation compete for floor time. For districts waiting on state dollars to finalize their own budgets, the delay adds another layer of fiscal uncertainty heading into the new school year.

summaries.headline: Michigan District Limits Teachers to 32 Approved Posters
summaries.summary: Romeo Community Schools, north of Detroit, now restricts teachers to a list of 32 pre-approved motivational phrases for classroom walls, with any other message requiring a four-step review process that includes legal counsel sign-off. Teachers and parents say the policy, which followed a board-passed ban on displays of "political ideology," targets imagery associated with LGBTQ acceptance—phrases like "Hate has no home here" and "All are welcome here" didn't make the approved list, even as anodyne quotes from Einstein or "Hang In There, Baby" posters now face bureaucratic scrutiny. The dispute mirrors a wider national pattern, tracked by PEN America since 2021, of states and districts moving to control classroom symbolism and language, with federal lawsuits in states like Ohio now testing how far those restrictions can legally reach.

summaries.headline: Chicago's Black Student Success Chief Reflects on Year One
summaries.summary: Eugene Robinson Jr., Chicago Public Schools' inaugural director of Black student success, spent his first year implementing a five-year plan he helped write while navigating community pressure for visible progress and a federal challenge from the Trump administration, which withheld funding over claims the plan discriminates against non-Black students. The rollout stayed low-key, marked by delays in seating a new Black Student Achievement Committee — the board only named most of its members this week, more than a year after Robinson took the role. Robinson, a CPS graduate from Englewood who previously led student engagement efforts and a UChicago charter campus, now faces the task of showing results as the district grapples with significant budget constraints and an ongoing legal fight over the plan's legitimacy.

summaries.headline: Final Memphis Audit Finds Mismanagement, Not Widespread Fraud
summaries.summary: A $6 million state audit of Memphis-Shelby County Schools found widespread breakdowns in recordkeeping and document management under previous administrations, but far less fraud than takeover proponents had predicted for months. The final report identified $54 million in spending flagged as fraud, waste, or abuse — about 1% of the district's 2021-2024 budget — with most of that tied to a single custodial contract canceled after one year, while a separate $65 million was found to violate district policy without breaking criminal law. The findings land as MSCS Superintendent Roderick Richmond faces a 45-day deadline to submit a corrective action plan, even as a federal judge has temporarily halted the state takeover the audit was meant to justify.

summaries.headline: Memphis Audit Finds $54 Million in Questionable Spending
summaries.summary: Tennessee's final forensic audit of Memphis-Shelby County Schools identified more than $54 million in spending showing evidence of potential fraud, waste, or abuse, with state Comptroller Jason Mumpower describing the findings as "systemic failures" in district management from 2021 to 2024 rather than isolated mistakes. A single custodial contract with ServiceMaster Clean accounts for over $48 million of that total, awarded in 2022 despite recommendations to split the work among multiple vendors, then canceled a year later after complaints about unclean schools and a whistleblower allegation of inflated costs tied to "kickbacks" that the district referred to the FBI. The report also flags more than $65 million in policy-violating spending and points to leadership turnover as a driver of fragmented recordkeeping and weak internal controls, landing just weeks before the school year starts and amid an ongoing legal fight over who will govern the district for the next four years.

summaries.headline: Chicago Names Black Student Achievement Committee, Two Years Late
summaries.summary: The Chicago Board of Education named a partial roster for its Black Student Achievement Committee, more than two years after Illinois lawmakers mandated the body and roughly a year after board members first promised to seat it. Board members Jitu Brown and Michilla Blaise, who will lead the group, screened a pool of 500 applicants before landing on members including a community organizer, a special education case manager, and an operations executive; the committee will now oversee rollout of the district's five-year Black Student Success Plan, which has already lost federal funding under scrutiny from the Trump administration. The repeated delays — first pushed from a September announcement, then through a reopened application process in December and January — have tested the patience of advocates watching to see whether the oversight structure can deliver results under national political pressure.

summaries.headline: Akron Board Begins Full-Year Superintendent Evaluation
summaries.summary: The Akron Board of Education kicked off a weeks-long evaluation of Superintendent Mary Outley and Treasurer Wayne Bowers, assessing their performance against goals set for the second half of the 2025-26 school year, including early literacy gains and budget management. Board President Barbara Sykes expects the process to stretch through most of July, with separate meetings for each administrator to revisit benchmarks and discuss any new goals, following a midyear review in February that found board members largely satisfied with both leaders' progress. The district pays outside consultant Leadership and Learning LLC $6,000 annually to facilitate the process, underscoring how formalized — and unhurried — superintendent accountability has become even for administrators whose contracts run through 2028.

# Breaking down literacy funding in state budget

## Michigan ranks 44th in reading

[Nick Monacelli](https://www.clickondetroit.com/team/KJTTSFXFAFHOVBSF74NN6VRVTA/ "View Nick Monacelli's author page"), Anchor/Reporter

Published: July 10, 2026 at 8:56 AM

[View comments](https://www.clickondetroit.com/news/local/2026/07/10/breaking-down-literacy-funding-in-state-budget/#commentDiv)

It’s been a week since the Michigan Legislature passed the state budget, and for parents and educators, there is a lot to know about what’s in it for schools.

Michigan schools are getting a 2.5% funding increase per student. That means a school gets $10,300 per student, compared to $10,500 last year.

All of that is part of the nearly $23 billion budget, and the focus: Literacy.

Michigan currently ranks 44th in the country in reading. The new budget is investing serious money to fix that—more funding for teacher training in reading methods, hiring literacy coaches, and expanding tutoring for students who are behind.

### So, who gets what?

The budget is working on a weighted system. That means some students get even more funding because they need more support. That includes students from low-income families, students with disabilities, and English language learners.

Free school meals for all students also continue.

And for teachers, some districts will be able to give pay increases. There is also more money for after-school programs, early childhood education, and career and technical education.

Lori Higgins with Chalkbeat Detroit, a non-profit news organization that covers education, joined Local 4 Live to talk more about this.

# 2026 IPA Congress Spotlights Children’s Books and Literacy

By Teri Tan

\|

The 35th International Publishers Association Congress, which was held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, concluded its two-day run on July 7. There were three sessions dedicated to children’s and YA publishing.

In “Bridging Worlds: Cross-Cultural Storytelling and Reading for the Next Generation,” moderator Simon de Jocas, a publishing consultant from Canada, discussed the current landscape of children’s literature and reading habits with Elena Pasoli, director of the Bologna Children’s Book Fair, and Ahmad Redza bin Ahmad Khairuddin, president of the Malaysia Board on Books for Young People (Malaysia IBBY).

“Keep giving children what they like to read, which is usually what they know or are familiar with,” advised Pasoli, who said that reading helped her get through one difficult childhood summer. “But make sure to introduce something else that they need or should know” Children, she said, “are known to feel lonely, and books connect them to the world. Reading lets them travel and know other worlds, thus increasing their sense of belonging and empathy.”

Ahmad Redza professed his initial disappointment in the reading choices of today’s young children. He related the story of wanting to pass down his own treasured collections of Enid Blyton’s The Famous Five and The Secret Seven series to his children. “They were totally not interested, not even in the new editions that I later bought. But they love the Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter,” he said. The world, he added, “has changed and so has the environment around children, who are spending a lot of their time in school. For me, so long as they are still reading, that’s good enough. That’s hopeful.”

As for further improving children’s publishing, Pasoli suggested that publishers talk to their counterparts in other countries, build bridges, and understand different experiences and perspectives. “This will make their books more innovative and appealing to a much wider audience. At the same time, the government sector needs to play a bigger role. Creating better citizens of tomorrow requires governments to support reading and publishers to view their role not through a narrow commercial lens but as an action for humanity.”

De Jocas pointed out that the oft-quoted statement about children’s attention spans getting shorter and their interest in books waning in the digital age is not necessarily corroborated by statistics.

Ahmad Redza, in turn, pointed out that “technology is neither a threat nor an evil. In fact, digital books make content accessible to children with special needs, which is great. So the digital format is not the issue; content is. We need good quality content in all formats to make reading interesting for children.”

In another breakout session, “Sustaining a Legacy: Half a Century of Children’s Publishing,” the spotlight fell on Gallimard Jeunesse, one of the world’s most iconic children’s publishers. CEO Hedwige Pasquet sat down with Karine Pansa, CEO of Grupo Girassol Brasil, to, in her words, “examine the past in order to meet the present and prepare for the future.”

In 2025, backlist—think _The Little Prince_, Beatrix Potter, Harry Potter, and titles by Roald Dahl—accounted for more than 64% of Gallimard Jeunesse’s total revenue of 52 million euros, of which six million euros came from international sales. Currently, one in every 10 titles sold to children and young adults around the globe is a Gallimard Jeunesse publication.

The company’s goals and values have remained the same since its establishment, Pasquet said. “It is about producing excellent quality content, conveying a sense of beauty through the illustrations—which is very important to children—and being creative and innovative in the publishing process to produce new formats and ways of enhancing content discoverability.” AI, Pasquet said, is mostly used in the company for marketing and promotional purposes, and not in the editorial process.

In recent years, Pasquet and her team have been busy building their YA program. “Through these titles, young adults can recognize themselves and read about the same issues that they and their counterparts are facing,” she said. “In short, we are helping the younger generation to grow and develop healthily to build the future society. This makes our publishing efforts even more meaningful.”

On the second day of the IPA Congress, the topic revolved around the deepening literary crisis. Hundreds of millions of children and young people are growing up without access to books. Sheikha Bodour Al Qasimi, the UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador for Education and Book Culture and founder of Kalimat Group and PublisHer, sat down for a fireside chat with moderator Emma House of Oreham Group to continue the discussion on reading for the future and the role of publishers in closing the global literacy gap.

“There is an abundance of publications out there, but in some parts of the world, there is a shortage of access for print and digital books, especially in refugee camps and areas without internet connectivity,” Sheikha Bodour said. “With books, refugees, for instance, can reimagine and plan their future path.”

But books, she said, “do not create readers. It is the reading culture that creates readers. And while AI is transforming how books are made, no algorithm ever falls in love with reading. But a human can. One book can change a life—I firmly believe that, and many publishers do, too. That is the power of a book.”

# Literacy Council partners with employers with free tutoring \| Opinion

## Mission is to build brighter futures by empowering adults, children, and families to acquire English literacy skills.

Dr. Leah Mason

July 10, 2026, 6:00 a.m. ET

[Share to Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=1703814913224751&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.naplesnews.com%2Fstory%2Fopinion%2F2026%2F07%2F10%2Fliteracy-council-partners-with-employers-with-free-tutoring-opinion%2F90858887007%2F)[Share to Twitter](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.naplesnews.com%2Fstory%2Fopinion%2F2026%2F07%2F10%2Fliteracy-council-partners-with-employers-with-free-tutoring-opinion%2F90858887007%2F&text=Literacy%20Council%20partners%20with%20employers%20with%20free%20tutoring%20%7C%20Opinion&via=ndn)[Share by email](mailto:?subject=Literacy%20Council%20partners%20with%20employers%20with%20free%20tutoring%20%7C%20Opinion%20-%20from%20Naples%20Daily%20News&body=Literacy%20Council%20partners%20with%20employers%20with%20free%20tutoring%20%7C%20Opinion%0A%0AMission%20is%20to%20build%20brighter%20futures%20by%20empowering%20adults%2C%20children%2C%20and%20families%20to%20acquire%20English%20literacy%20skills.%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20naplesnews.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.naplesnews.com%2Fstory%2Fopinion%2F2026%2F07%2F10%2Fliteracy-council-partners-with-employers-with-free-tutoring-opinion%2F90858887007%2F)

- A 2025 study by National University found that 45 million U.S. adults are functionally illiterate.
- The Literacy Council Gulf Coast partners with local employers to provide on-site English instruction.
- Bonita National Golf & Country Club offers a worksite literacy program where resident members tutor employees.
- The program has helped employees improve their English skills, pursue citizenship, and build community.

National University found in 2025 that approximately 45 million U.S. adults are functionally illiterate and read below a fifth-grade level. Literacy skills are essential for daily life, which means 45 million people are struggling to read, comprehend, or even communicate with others.

The Literacy Council Gulf Coast’s mission is to build brighter futures by empowering adults, children, and families to acquire English literacy skills and education to enhance their quality of life. Our worksite literacy program partners with local employers to provide on-site English instruction, where employees gain the essential language and communication skills that open doors to greater career opportunities and personal growth.

We’ve been partners with Bonita National Golf & Country Club for two years, to provide free one-on-one tutoring to 25 of its employees. Each program runs differently depending on needs and operations of the business.

Leslie Starsoncek, a resident of Bonita National, learned about the worksite literacy program and brought it to the attention of management. The management is very supportive and allows employees to receive tutoring during their shifts. What sets the program apart is that all the volunteer tutors are residents or members of Bonita National. Each week employees have a 1 to 2 hour 1:1 tutoring session.

Starsoneck believes that the relationship and trust built between employees and resident tutors has contributed to the success of the program. Students are also given the ability to share learned skills with their family and closer community.

Membership and Lifestyle Director at Bonita National, Gabrielle Kreller, said she has seen impact through every step of the program. It provides a sense of community and belonging for its staff members.

“The club industry is all about member expectations and really, we’re here for the members, but also the members are here for the staff. So, we want to bring in and create a culture that everyone enjoys,” Kreller said.

The program has created a ripple effect in the employees' personal lives.

One staff member is using the literacy skills to work toward their citizenship, and is bringing the knowledge home to their children, to teach them English.

Kreller said the most impactful memory was hearing a student, and staff member, read aloud a thank you letter he wrote to the tutors and Bonita National management.

“It was giving us all goosebumps because it really was a huge impact because he was able to write in English, speak in English and read as well,” Kreller said.

We hope that our community understands the importance and impact our programs have. Literacy is an essential skill for a functional and thriving society. Literacy is not just the ability to communicate, it's to learn and succeed. The Literacy Council Gulf Coast is here to break down barriers and create opportunities for our Southwest Florida community. Literacy changes lives, strengthens families, and builds a more vibrant community for us all. Whether you're an employer, a volunteer, or someone looking to support this mission, now is the time to get involved. Together, we can ensure that everyone has the opportunity to learn, grow, and thrive.

If you want to support the work of the Literacy Council Gulf Coast join us at our inaugural Tee up For Literacy golf tournament, on Saturday October 3 at Stoneybrook Golf Club. To register or learn more about sponsorship opportunities contact me at leah@literacycouncilgulfcoast.org, call 239-676-5202, or visit our website at https://literacygulfcoast.org/.

_Dr. Leah Mason is executive director of the Literacy Council Gulf Coast._

![](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.ironmountaindailynews.com/images/2026/07/03144813/Michigah-House-1100x734.jpg)

LANSING — Michigan’s fiscal year 2027 budget that was passed Friday morning includes new investments in student literacy and continued funding for other priorities, according to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

State Rep. Greg Markkanen, R-Hancock, in a news release Friday said the budget locks in critical funding for first responders and schools. It includes no new taxes, strengthens accountability measures and focuses on efficiency in state department spending, he said.

Lawmakers worked through the night Thursday to finalize the $84 billion spending plan for the fiscal year that begins Oct. 1.

According to Bridge Michigan, the budget boosts spending on targeted initiatives, especially programs aimed at helping improve poor student reading scores. It includes $65 million in additional funding for Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading and Spelling teacher literacy training, $10.5 million in extra funding for literacy coaches, $50 million for “high-impact tutoring” grants and $30 million early learning partnerships.

“Governor Whitmer once again brought Democrats and Republicans together to pass a bipartisan, balanced budget that will lower costs, help our kids succeed, and protect Medicaid,” State Budget Director Jen Flood said Friday in a news release.

![](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.ironmountaindailynews.com/images/2019/08/20112355/GregMarkkanen-600x840.jpg)

GREG MARKKANEN

The state expects food stamp work requirements will save the state $71 million as the number of recipients declines, Bridge MIchigan reported. However, implementing work requirements for SNAP and Medicaid is expected to cost the state nearly as much.

The governor’s office citied the following savings for residents in the budget:

— $200 million to continue free school meals for all 1.4 million public school students, saving families about $1,000 per year, per child.

— Continuing the Working Families Tax Credit, sending an average of nearly $3,900 in tax relief to 665,000 families.

— Rolling back the retirement tax completely, saving 500,000 seniors an average of $1,000 a year.

![](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.ironmountaindailynews.com/images/2026/07/05180708/Karl-Bohnak-fixed-600x840.jpg)

KARL BOHNAK

Continuing tax exemptions include:

— Tips (saving 300,000 workers $400 a year),

— Overtime (saving 500,000 workers $500 a year),

— Social Security (saving 40,000 seniors $500 a year)

— $5 million for water affordability, helping families pay their bills and avoiding water shut offs.

— $5 million for weatherization to help families lower their utility bills.

Regarding K-12 education, the governor’s office said the budget includes:

— $325 million to support school operations through a 2.5% increase in base per-pupil funding — an additional $250 per student, for a total of $10,300 per pupil. The per-pupil funding represents  a  31% increase since Whitmer took office, the governor’s office said.

— $123 million to continue expanded support for special education students – a 7.3% increase in the state allocation.

— $278 million, to provide a 20% increase in funding to support academically at-risk students and English language learners, and a 10% increase in funding to support career and technical education students, and students in rural school districts.

— Up to $321 million to support student wellness through continuation of mental health and safety grants to districts.

— $125 million to reimburse districts with exorbitant transportation costs, allowing them to devote more resources to the classroom.

— $30 million to support early learning partnerships, ensuring students and families access to high-quality early learning and updated GSR programs statewide.

— $40 million to reimburse eligible districts for dual enrollment costs, incentivizing districts to encourage more students to pursue college credit while still in high school.

— $2.4 million increase for Early On services, bringing total funding to $26.1 million. Early On is Michigan’s system that connects families of infants and toddlers from birth to age 3 who have, or are at risk for, developmental delays or disabilities with coordinated social, health, and educational services to support early development.

For higher education, the budget includes:

— $2.2 billion to sustain university and community college operations–advancing Michigan’s Sixty by 30 goal of having 60% of working adults with a degree or skills certificate by 2030.

— $532 million, and more than $1.7 billion to date, for the Michigan Achievement Scholarship, which provides a tuition free pathway for full-time community college students through the community college guarantee, and up to $27,500 for full-time students at public or private four-year universities. More than 106,300 students have been awarded the Michigan Achievement Scholarship since its inception in 2024, and 128,000 students are expected to benefit each year once the program is fully implemented.

— $25 million to support expanding Michigan Reconnect to adult learners ages 21 and older, giving adult learners a tuition-free pathway to earn an associate degree or skilled trades certificate. More than 66,500 students have enrolled in community college with Michigan Reconnect since it was created in 2021.

— $1.3 billion in total capital outlay project authorizations for 27 of the state’s higher education institutions, with a state cost participation of $524.3 million.

Markkanen said the budget includes $30 million for infrastructure improvements at Michigan Technological University in Houghton. The funding will go to support a Center for Convergence and Innovation.

“Michigan Technological University is one of the Upper Peninsula’s greatest assets, and these infrastructure improvements will help ensure it continues attracting talented students, researchers, and employers to our region,” Markkanen said. “Investing in Michigan Tech is an investment in our local economy, our workforce, and the future of the U.P. This funding will strengthen innovation while creating opportunities that benefit students and the surrounding communities alike.”

State Rep. Karl Bohnak, R-Deerton, said the budget ensures that local scheduled road and bridge repairs statewide are fully funded for next year.

In a news release Friday, Bohnak said the budget also delivers three significant local funding investments he championed for the Upper Peninsula. The projects include $682,000 for the Baraga County Road Commission, $500,000 for the 906 Adventure Team, and $35,000 for the United Way of Marquette County.

Bohnak said he will share additional details about each investment in the coming days.

Warwick added that “Heritage Action applauds the Board’s leadership in advancing a curriculum that celebrates our history rather than apologizing for it.”

Other measures approved by the [Texas](https://www.dailysignal.com/2026/07/06/texas-combat-birth-tourism/) board include language to strengthen English reading and proficiency curricula and update the social studies standards of Essential Knowledge and Skills of the Texas Education Code by adopting newly passed state legislative bills.

Other measures adopted by the board include implementing Texas’ House Bill 27 into the state curriculum, which adds a half-credit requirement for [personal financial literacy](https://www.dailysignal.com/2025/03/16/how-this-couple-transformed-their-financial-life-by-aligning-their-money-with-their-faith/).

[House Bill 824](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/analysis/html/HB00824H.htm) mandates that classrooms include specific civic instruction in high school government courses. The new curriculum also mandates lessons on election laws, government official roles, running for office, and Robert’s Rules of Order.

In a statement posted on X, Chairman of the Texas State Board of Education Aaron Kinsey “ [praised](https://x.com/AaronKinseyTX/status/2070691193684382054)” the new measures as an opportunity to give the next generation of students to “trace the development of liberty, self-government, free enterprise, and constitutional principles across generations.”

“Students will finally get the full story,” the chairman added. “This is how historians work.”

“Students will see how people, ideas, events, and institutions influenced one another across time rather than studying them as separate topics,” he continued.

These newly adopted measures expand on the ones previously adopted by the state board under the leadership of Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.

Last year, for instance, the Texas State Board adopted Senate Bill 10, which mandates that each public classroom display a framed poster or copy at least 16 by 20 inches in size, with readable text, of the [Ten Commandments](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/05/24/ten-commandments-texas-schools-senate-bill-10/).
